name: Back of Beyond Ranch
description: 1849: a mountain trading post on a ridge that, by later local tradition, Kit Carson named West Point in 1844 while hunting a Sierra pass. The place was called Indian Gulch first — Northern Sierra Miwok ground, busy before anyone yelled gold. The guest book already has names that do not match the faces. (Later: the landmark plaque will say Bret Harte lived at West Point for a time. Now: this cabin is Back of Beyond Ranch.)

name: Angels Camp
description: 1849: Henry Pinkney Angell’s trading post from 1848, still a creek camp of tents around the store. Miners already wager on frogs. The gold is creek placer. (Later: quartz mining from 1854; stone Angels Hotel 1855; Ben Coon tells Sam Clemens the frog tale in 1865; Jumping Frog Jubilee from 1928. Now: City of Angels, the museum, Frogtown.)

name: Murphys
description: 1849: John and Daniel Murphy’s gulch from 1848 — muddy street, tents, barrels. French and Italian men are already talking vines. (Later: Murphys Historic Hotel from 1856; a register that, by local tradition, will hold Twain, Grant, and Black Bart. Now: Visit Murphys, the hotel, Mercer Caverns, Ironstone next door.)

name: Moaning Cavern
description: 1849: miners named this hole for the moan at the mouth. Some drop on ropes for color; others will not go in. Bone is already underfoot — no one here can date it. (Later: a main room with a 165-foot drop, billed by its operator as the largest single cave chamber in California; spiral-stair tours from 1922; remains put at 12,000 years or more by one 1950s estimate, far younger by another. Now: Moaning Caverns cave tours.)

name: California Caverns
description: The Mother Lode's great show cave, found by miners in October 1850 beside the camp later called Cave City. Its winding passages hide rare aragonite crystal formations and an underground lake, and tours have run here since the Gold Rush era — and later John Muir explored the caverns and wrote about their crystal-hung chambers (in print 1876). (Now: beyond the lighted walking route, wild sections still require crawling, wading, and rafting to reach.) Plenty of dark corners for a fugitive to stash what shouldn't be found.

name: Calaveras Big Trees
description: Home of the giant sequoias that made the world gasp. When the 'Discovery Tree' was found here in 1852, people back East refused to believe a tree could be that big — so promoters felled the 1,200-year-old giant and toured pieces of it as proof. Thirty-two people once danced a cotillion on the leveled stump, which still sits near the North Grove trailhead today. The groves outlived their exploiters: these trees were already ancient before the Gold Rush, before the missions, before almost everything.

name: The ridge above Jackson
description: 1849: placer on the ridge above Botilleas. Black miners were on this hill first. A hole is being sunk that the claim book does not explain, and a canvas meat stall feeds it. (Later: Kennedy quartz 1856+, company 1860, workings 5,912 ft deep by 1942; Ellis Evans butcher in town by 1850; Swingle Meat 1945 on Kennedy Flat. The 1922 fire that killed 47 was the neighboring Argonaut.)

name: Mokelumne Hill
description: 1849: one of the richest and meanest camps in the southern mines. Claims limited to sixteen feet square. French, Chilean, and American tents on one slope, already not sharing it. (Later: a killing every weekend for 17 weeks, says an 1881 county history that gives no year; the French War of 1851; the Hotel de France 1851, later the Léger; fires 1854, 1864 or 1865, 1874. Now: the Léger still open, GoCalaveras Mokelumne Hill guide.)

name: Ironstone Vineyards
description: A winery estate in Gold Rush style, with gardens, tasting cellars, and a museum holding the Mother Lode's most jaw-dropping treasure: a 44-pound mass of crystalline gold leaf, believed to be the largest specimen of its kind, unearthed in 1992 at a mine near Jamestown. After a century and a half of picks, pans, and dredges, what may be the greatest piece of crystalline gold ever found sits behind glass just minutes from Murphys — exactly the sort of prize a thief might find irresistible.

name: Jackson
description: 1849: a camp at a spring of empty bottles — Botilleas. Main Street is mud, not brick. Chinese miners are already cutting a way under it. Warrants are a man’s word.

name: Natural Bridges
description: A hidden geological wonder near Vallecito, where Coyote Creek spent millions of years dissolving a band of limestone — carving caves whose roofs finally collapsed, leaving the creek flowing beneath massive natural stone arches. Gold Rush miners worked these gravels for placer gold; today a short trail drops to a swimming hole where, on a hot summer day, you can float right under the arch through a cool, formation-hung cavern. Pack water shoes and a flashlight, and watch the gravel bars — color still turns up in a pan now and then.

sites.name: Natural Bridges trail (GoCalaveras / USBR New Melones)

name: Volcano
description: One of the richest placer camps in the southern mines, born in 1849 as 'Soldiers Gulch' after men of Colonel Stevenson's New York regiment struck color here the year before. The camp sits in a crater-like limestone basin, and the morning mist that rises from it gave the town its name — there is no volcano. In these early days it is a raw sprawl of tents and canvas stores, its gravels famously rich (a hundred dollars a day was common talk) and growing richer the deeper they were dug, the gold caught in potholes worn into the limestone. The southern mines are astonishingly mixed — Sonoran and Chilean placer men, Anglo-Americans, and the Northern Sierra Miwok on whose homeland it all unfolds.
